doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: European audiences, Amsterdam and Berlin
summary: Raph recalls warm European audiences and photographers on stage in Amsterdam. He tells of a trip to East Berlin and of East Berliners leaving the Sports Palace early because of curfew.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Most guys say that the audiences in Europe were different. Did you find that to be true?
Now we are talking forty years ago.

Okay? I don’t know how they are now. But in those days they were all — the audiences were very demonstrative and very appreciative of what you did. Very responsive. Warmer perhaps than some other audiences. But we went to Amsterdam for instance. We played there where the Concertgebouw Orchestra plays, it’s a round stage. I think it’s completely surrounded by audience if I remember. Well the photographers were on stage during the concert shooting flash bulbs in our eyes. And I remember Brookmeyer almost beating them away with his trombone. That was different. I hadn’t seen that before. We had one very interesting experience at the Sports Palace in Berlin. This was 1961 I believe. Of course the war was over in ’45. The Berlin Wall was still up. And I had a personal experience — I took the train from West Berlin to East Berlin. I got off way out in East Berlin. I wanted to make sure I was there because I couldn’t tell by the map if I was passing the Brandenburg Gate or not. But I got off in East Berlin. And I had a heck of a time getting back because I didn’t have any East German money. So I had to go to a store that couldn’t sell me a camera because I didn’t have the passport or I didn’t have the right papers, and a guy from the store walked me a couple of blocks to some money changer where they changed a couple of dollars worth of west money to east money and I was able to get back. But it was scary for a minute. At the Sports Palace, which I started to say, we played a concert and I guess the concert normal length was about two hours. So we were finishing it up, we had one or two encores that we were going to play. But after we did the last number, instead of applauding, half the audience got up and left. They just left. And we couldn’t understand this. We found out later that these people were from East Berlin. They had a curfew. And they already stayed past their curfew. So if they all left together they had a chance of getting back to East Berlin without facing the authorities. So they all got up en masse and left. It was the weirdest thing. We thought they enjoyed the concert and here they are running out.
But they gave you a pretty high compliment by staying that late.
Oh yeah, they did. They actually stayed past their curfew because they were so interested in the music.
